rationale: Three independent randomized human trials outside Parkinson disease report lower visual-analogue pain with encapsulated oral cinnamon bark powder versus starch placebo in primary dysmenorrhea (n=114, 24-72 h), migraine (n=43 completers, p<.001), and rheumatoid arthritis (n=36, abstract p<.001), alongside a high-attrition multiple-sclerosis trial with baseline imbalance and endpoint switch (VAS vs registered PQAS). Competing controlled trials show null upper abdominal pain for cinnamon-sesame macerate versus sesame oil and inconsistent exercise-soreness findings, while the single Parkinson rehabilitation case combined cassia with multimodal therapy. One oral ground Ceylon cinnamon experiment in female rats found smaller bladder-distension reflexes with induced cystitis and larger responses in uninflamed bladders at the same higher dose. The mixed animal proxy supplies no transferable sign. Differences in culinary ground exposure, non-Parkinson pain etiologies, and reporting limits keep the favorable easing signal at minimal_signal. An identified Cinnamomum burmannii extract in a cellular screen supplies preparation context without a pain-severity or Parkinson observation. Cinnamon is an identification odor in the acute-illness comparison. The paper has no assigned culinary cinnamon pain treatment or attributable pain contrast. The review lists cinnamon as one source of eugenol. Isolated-eugenol trials have chemical, thermal and motor results in rodents, with controlled human oral cinnamon evidence still the closest basis. The new experiment concerns an isolated cinnamon constituent in an animal model with intestinal outcomes. Ground cinnamon and clinical Parkinson pain were not assessed. A traceable Chinese consensus passage recommends a compound cinnamon-twig formula with kudzu as one patterned pain option. Its recommendation supplies no measured result for ground cinnamon in people with Parkinson disease. An extract adjunct trial in H. pylori treatment reports lower short-term epigastric-pain prevalence (p=.02 in Table 2), while a different combined cinnamon leaf tea pilot reports transient colicky pain without a quantified comparison. The contexts and exposures limit transfer to ground bark and Parkinson pain.

No controlled clinical comparison establishes an anxiety effect for cold-pressed flaxseed oil. An oil-alone human anxiety trial (DOI10.23937/2474-3631/1510010) found an inconclusive final Beck anxiety contrast (p=.31) with low baseline scores and unverified pressing. Parkinson omega-3 plus vitamin-E trials report no isolated anxiety item or oil-only arm, and rodent elevated-plus-maze proxies (rotenone, maternal separation with null light-dark and higher amygdala inflammation, haloperidol oil-alone null) do not supply an eligible clinical sign. The claim therefore moves from legacy 51 to open. A newer randomized migraine study reported a larger DASS-21 anxiety decrease with flaxseed oil plus L-carnitine than placebos. It cannot separate the two active ingredients or establish the effect of cold-pressed oil in Parkinson disease.

No controlled comparison against an inactive control isolates cold-pressed flaxseed oil for constipation severity. The registered hemodialysis trial (NCT02103556, PMID25238699) compared flaxseed, olive, and active laxative mineral oil (n=50) and found an inconclusive between-oil interaction (p=.15) with unverified pressing grade; a lipid trial (sjams.2018.v06i01.047) logged 2/57 vs 5/55 constipation adverse events against liquid paraffin without severity scoring; plasma ALA was unrelated to Wexner constipation (PMID34127758); and petroleum-ether extracted oil gave a nonmonotonic rodent wet-stool response. Consistent with claim 0072, the claim moves from legacy 51 to open. Two placebo or active-control studies report bowel improvements from flaxseed baked into cookies or prepared as flour. These seed-containing foods provide no isolated flaxseed oil comparison.

One randomized intention-to-treat trial in 68 adults with migraine (PMID41478596, IRCT20230616058497N1) reports greater eight-week Insomnia Severity Index reduction with oral flaxseed powder versus roasted wheat powder (-4.6 vs -1.6, p=.029) alongside headache-severity improvement. An uncontrolled 46-student pilot of roasted whole flaxseed (DOI10.5455/jrtm.2022/97416) found shorter polysomnography sleep latency (p<.001), inconclusive global PSQI (p=.635), and a text-versus-table Epworth Sleepiness Scale discrepancy without a comparison arm. Powdered whole seed rather than cold-pressed flaxseed oil and a migraine rather than Parkinson cohort keep the easing signal at minimal_signal. The flaxseed-oil and carnitine results article reports no PSQI estimate for the registered sleep outcome.

A controlled ground-cinnamon crossover outside Parkinson disease had no clear daily stool-frequency contrast. Human cassia water-extract findings concern model-relevant transit during diarrhea. Extract experiments in constipated and diarrheal rats move pellet frequency in different directions under different conditions. The symptom-severity direction remains unresolved. The 2017 iRBD study used cinnamon as one odor in an aggregate smell-identification test. It assessed baseline constipation separately. The diagnostic setting supplies no constipation comparison attributed to cinnamon. In a randomized extract adjunct trial, the Table 2 constipation comparison was inconclusive (11 to 6 versus 18 to 15 of 49, p=.10), despite the abstract grouping it with significant results. A combined leaf tea reports qualitative bowel improvement without an attributable comparison. Koyna Valley traditions describe root paste for constipation and use ground bark for a different symptom.
